sop.coo_evaluation:
# **Gaps — no SOP yet**

- **Member onboarding** – no documented journey from signup → first class → integration into community (assessment, goal-setting, buddy assignment, comms cadence all ad-hoc)
- **Cancellation & churn** – no win-back protocol, exit interview process, or trigger-based retention campaigns
- **Coaching development & progression** – no roadmap for how coaches level up, get certified in new formats, or transition to senior/mentor roles
- **Class quality audit** – no standardised observation/feedback loop to maintain consistency across coaches and peak times
- **Member data privacy & GDPR** – critical gap given UK gym context; no consent workflows, data retention, or breach response documented
- **Weekly key coach tasks** – no playbook for what coaches own beyond class delivery (comms, check-ins, reporting)
- **Pause/freeze protocol** – no clear SOP for members stepping back temporarily (billing, re-engagement, duration rules)
- **Referral programme** – no mechanism to activate existing members as advocates or track referral outcomes
- **Order supplies & sundries** – no inventory, vendor, or reorder thresholds defined
- **Complaints & incidents** – no escalation path, documentation standard, or resolution timeframe

---

# **Needs updating**

- **Member check-ins** (exists but likely surface-level) – add triggers for at-risk members, frequency rules by tenure/attendance, and coach accountability
- **Milestone achievements & 30-day goals** – currently separate; merge into single progress-tracking SOP with celebration/communication protocol
- **Member outcomes** – lacks connection to initial goals; needs measurement framework (strength, confidence, community belonging) and quarterly review cadence
- **Marketing SOPs (5/5)** – assume these pre-date paid referral or ambassador schemes; audit for integration with new refer

kpi.advice:
# The Forge — Fractional CFO Advice

## REVENUE — THE PRIORITY

• **Churn spike in May (12.8%) is your biggest leak.** You had 134 members but lost 17; that's £2,040 annualised revenue walking out the door in one month. Investigate: post-relocation discomfort? Pricing resistance? Compare May joiners vs. leavers by cohort. Target: hold churn under 5% (your April/June baseline). Action: member feedback survey + 1-to-1 calls with May churn cohort this week.

• **Revenue per member flat-lining at £118–£139 despite 134 members in July.** You're not upselling. Check: are card packages (PT, classes, supplements) being offered at sign-up and in app? July's £19.8k on 143 members (£138/member) is your best. Replicate that by introducing a tiered "class pass add-on" (+£15–25/month) at onboarding and pushing existing members to upgrade via WhatsApp/email. Target: £145/member average by October.

• **Summer growth (143 members in July) is real.** Exploit it: launch a "bring a friend free week" in August–September (peak holiday season) and lock in 3-month commitment discounts. Don't let July's momentum die.

---

## EXPENSES — WHERE TO LOOK

• **Cash burn in March (–£5.3k) and April (planned, exclude) shows payroll or supplies spiking.** Review March payroll: was there a bonus, maternity cover, or one-off cost? July was lean (–£8.1k net cash *in*). Baseline monthly cash out should be ~£17–18k. If staffing is variable, tie hours to member count (target: 12–14 staff FTE equivalent for 140 members); avoid fixed overstaffing.

• **Supplier audit:** March and May outflows (£23.3k, £16.6k) included non-relocation costs. Itemise: utilities, equipment maintenance, insurance, cleaning, rent. Negotiate annual fixed-rate energy deal (energy bills likely 8–12% of revenue — check if you're on a business tariff). Cleaning and laundry: if outsourced, get 3 quotes; if in-house, measure cost per member per month.

---

## PROFITABILITY & TAX

• **On 7-month run (excl. April), you're averaging £15.6k revenue/month with ~£18k

class_stats.suggestion:
**Fill quiet studio time:**

1. Add a paid "Open Gym + Form Check" slot on Thursday afternoons (your quietest day) — 30 mins where members can lift freely with a coach available for quick technique questions, targeting the gap between classes and capturing members who want flexibility without full-class commitment.

2. Launch a Saturday morning "Barbell Fundamentals" workshop (30–45 mins) before or after existing classes — teaches proper setup and common fixes for Build class newcomers, directly feeds people into Barbelle and Engine who may be intimidated by those classes solo.

**Lift the quieter classes:**

3. Run a 2-week "try Capacity/Engine/Strongevity free" campaign targeting your Build class regulars via email with a specific hook per class — e.g. "Build got you strong, now build your work capacity" for Engine — and schedule these as back-to-back options on Tuesday/Wednesday when attendance is highest, so members can test them when the gym's busy.

kpis.Action: INTERNAL: Create clear service menu (for coaches and for members) — what we offer, what it costs, what's included.
kpis.advice:
# Service Menu Execution for The Forge

• **Start with your revenue reality, not aspirations.** Audit what your coaches *actually* deliver now (group classes, PT sessions, nutrition checks, form assessments) and what members are *currently* paying for or asking about. Build the menu from existing demand, then add gaps. Don't invent services hoping to sell them.

• **Build two separate docs, not one.** Coach menu = clear pricing tiers, what they can/can't sell, commission or margin structures, which services they own vs. cross-sell. Member menu = benefits by membership tier, add-on costs, bundled vs. à la carte (e.g., 5-session PT block at £X vs. pay-per-session). Coaches need operational clarity; members need simple buying logic.

• **Price by perceived value to women, not cost-plus guessing.** "Women's-only fitness" attracts members willing to pay premium for psychology/comfort benefits. Test a PT session at £45-55 (not £35) if competitors charge £40. Members will justify it. Price the nutrition audit high (£60+) even if it's 30 mins—it solves a real pain point. Then test uptake.

• **Lock in a 2-week rollout.** Week 1: internal coach feedback on draft menu (resolve confusion, fix gaps). Week 2: launch to members via email + in-gym posters. Don't over-polish it—you'll iterate. Getting feedback from real sales attempts beats workshop meetings.

• **Assign one person (probably you) to own updates quarterly.** Service menus die when they become "someone's project." You own it, you update it when coaching

• **Start with your revenue reality, not aspirations.** Audit what your coaches *actually* deliver now (group classes, PT sessions, nutrition checks, form assessments) and what members are *currently* paying for or asking about. Build the menu from existing demand, then add gaps. Don't invent services hoping to sell them.

• **Build two separate docs, not one.** Coach menu = clear pricing tiers, what they can/can't sell, commission or margin structures, which services they own vs. cross-sell. Member menu = benefits by membership tier, add-on costs, bundled vs. à la carte (e.g., 5-session PT block at £X vs. pay-per-session). Coaches need operational clarity; members need simple buying logic.

• **Price by perceived value to women, not cost-plus guessing.** "Women's-only fitness" attracts members willing to pay premium for psychology/comfort benefits. Test a PT session at £45-55 (not £35) if competitors charge £40. Members will justify it. Price the nutrition audit high (£60+) even if it's 30 mins—it solves a real pain point. Then test uptake.

• **Lock in a 2-week rollout.** Week 1: internal coach feedback on draft menu (resolve confusion, fix gaps). Week 2: launch to members via email + in-gym posters. Don't over-polish it—you'll iterate. Getting feedback from real sales attempts beats workshop meetings.

• **Assign one person (probably you) to own updates quarterly.** Service menus die when they become "someone's project." You own it, you update it when coaching

**Insights**

1. **July was an anomaly—August is the real baseline.** You spent less (£355 vs £515) and got fewer leads (78 vs 215), but your CPL doubled (£5 vs £2) and close rate held (31% vs 13%). July's £2 CPL was unsustainably cheap; the leads were likely low-intent volume. August's £5 CPL with 31% conversion is your genuine performance floor and shows the quality/quantity trade-off has normalized.

2. **Spring collapse into July recovery tells a story.** Apr–Jun you were hemorrhaging efficiency (CPL climbed £6→£14→£21) with zero sales—classic sign of wrong audience targeting, poor creative decay, or lead quality so bad your sales team gave up following up. July's pivot (new creative? audience reset? sales process fix?) worked immediately. August proves it stuck, but the lead volume dropped 64% month-on-month without a spend cut, suggesting either audience saturation or that July's winning approach is already losing steam.

3. **Profitability is fragile on thin margins.** At £28 income per trial (guessing £175–200 trial fee ÷ 24 sales), you're making £65 profit total in August on £355 spend. That's 18% margin. One bad month of conversion or CPL creep puts you underwater. You need either higher close rates, lower CPL, or both.

**Actions**

1. **Immediately audit and rebuild your lead follow-up process.** You closed 31% in August (24/78) but only 13% in July (29/215). That's not random—it's sales capacity or qualification hitting a wall. Before spending more, confirm: are you phoning leads same-day? If August leads converted better, reverse-engineer what made them different and instruct your ad account to only find similar intent signals.
